extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, and psychologists interested in the process of mathematical creativity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observations about how mathematical invention occurs: the interplay of conscious work, unconscious (subliminal) incubation, intuition of order, aesthetic sensibility, and verification. Focused on practices and mental conditions that lead to insight and on individual differences in capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of unconscious (subliminal) work in invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The unconscious (subliminal self) plays an important rôle in mathematical creation; sudden illuminations arise after prolonged unconscious processing and present ideas with immediacy and certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré reports that decisive ideas often appear 'sudden[ly]' and with 'perfect certainty' after a period of unconscious work; these inspirations are manifestations of prior unconscious processing rather than purely conscious invention. Expect insight to feel immediate and convincing, and view such moments as fruits of prior unconscious activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious work must precede unconscious incubation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden inspirations never happen except after some days of voluntary effort which has appeared fruitless; preliminary conscious work mobilizes the material the unconscious will recombine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate, effortful work (exploring dead-ends, trying many combinations) is a necessary precondition: it 'sets agoing the unconscious machine.' Don't rely on passive waiting for ideas — do directed work first to prime incubation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up conscious work (verification and formalization) is required
rubrics_metrics.description: After inspiration a second period of conscious work is necessary to put the idea in shape: verify, deduce consequences, arrange and word demonstrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat inspiration as a starting point, not a finished proof. The unconscious typically provides a 'point of departure' while the detailed, disciplined calculations and rigorous proofs must be carried out consciously; many sudden ideas must be tested and sometimes fail verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition of order — perceiving the proof as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical demonstration is not just juxtaposed syllogisms but syllogisms placed in a certain order; the intuition or feeling of this order allows one to grasp the reasoning as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate the sense of the global structure of an argument: the order of elements often matters more than any one element. This intuition lets one reconstruct or re-invent a proof without relying solely on mechanical memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory and attention vs. intuition — different routes to competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Special aptitude may come from very sure memory or prodigious attention (enabling retention of long chains), but true creation depends on the intuition of order; some who can learn and apply but not create rely on memory/attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize two complementary capacities: mechanical memory/attention supports retention and application, whereas the delicate intuitive grasp of order enables invention. Training can bolster memory and technique, but creation often needs that intuitive ordering ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic sensibility as the selective sieve
rubrics_metrics.description: A special esthetic sensibility — the feeling of mathematical beauty, harmony and elegance — acts as the delicate sieve that selects which unconscious combinations become conscious; the useful combinations are precisely the most beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value elegance and harmonious organization as heuristics: ideas that 'charm' the mathematician are more likely to be fruitful. Note that aesthetic appeal can also mislead; false inspirations often nevertheless 'gratified our natural feeling for mathematical elegance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention = discernment (choosing useful combinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: To create is not merely to make new combinations (which anyone could do) but to avoid useless combinations and select the few that are useful; invention is essentially discernment and choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus effort on recognizing analogies and relations that suggest general laws, rather than generating many arbitrary combinations. Practice evaluating potential combinations for their capacity to reveal deeper structure or laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fertility often comes from combining distant domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Among chosen combinations the most fertile will often be those formed of elements drawn from domains which are far apart; rare cross-domain links reveal unsuspected kinships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage cross-disciplinary analogies and looking for analogies between seemingly unrelated areas, while being aware that most very disparate combinations will be sterile — seek the rare ones that expose deep kinship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of elements is more important than individual steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The order in which reasoning elements are placed is much more important than the elements themselves; having the feeling of this order prevents losing elements through memory failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or writing proofs, emphasize the organizing principles and order (the 'march of the reasoning') so learners can reconstruct details even if they forget intermediate steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and fallibility of sudden illumination
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden illuminations are characterized by brevity, suddenness and immediate certainty; usually they do not deceive, but sometimes the feeling of certitude is vivid while false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sudden certainty with healthy skepticism: always follow with careful verification. Expect most inspirations to be correct but verify because some convincing intuitions fail upon attempted formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious work seldom produces finished long calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious work does not produce the result of a somewhat long calculation made entirely; one may hope only for a point of departure for such calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on dreams or incubation to deliver completed computations or detailed algebra; plan to carry out explicit computations consciously after an insight supplies the strategy or starting point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest and change of activity facilitate unconscious processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Rest, travel, or diversion often allow unconscious ideas to assemble and lead to insight (examples include ideas arising on walks, in omnibus, or while on geological excursions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build breaks and changes of scenery into problem-solving: an interruption can permit unconscious recombination that yields an insight later; purposeful temporary disengagement is a productive strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary conscious work mobilizes relevant 'elements' (atoms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscious preliminary work 'unhooks' and mobilizes certain elements (likened to atoms) so they can move during unconscious incubation and form useful combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in directed exploration to ensure the unconscious has the right material to recombine: targeted attempts mobilize relevant concepts and increase the probability that unconscious combinations will include useful parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual differences: not everyone will be a creator
rubrics_metrics.description: Some lack the delicate feeling/intuition or sufficient memory/attention and thus are incapable of understanding higher mathematics or becoming creators; abilities vary in degree across individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge different profiles: some learners may become competent through memorization and application, others may develop creative intuition; pedagogical approaches should account for these differences and cultivate both technique and aesthetic sense where possible.
